mountain-home-state-forest.intro: Two giant sequoias in Mountain Home Grove take their names from the first pages of Genesis, and they had very different fires. Genesis, once ranked seventh among the largest trees known, lost its top in the 2020 Castle Fire and was badly burned at the base. The Adam Tree, named around 1884 and measured at 29 metres round in 1978, came through with a blackened base and little else. The grove sits in a state demonstration forest above Springville, free to enter and a long mountain drive from anywhere.
mountain-home-state-forest.meta_description: Mountain Home Grove holds Genesis, once the seventh-largest tree known, burned in the 2020 Castle Fire, and the Adam Tree, named around 1884.
mountain-home-state-forest.question_answer: The tree Mountain Home is known for is Genesis, a giant sequoia that ranked seventh among the largest trees known before the 2020 Castle Fire. Its last full measurement, from 2013, gave it 86.2 metres of height and 24.04 metres of girth, figures that date from before the fire took its top and burned its base. Visitors in 2021 found it badly damaged but alive, and nothing more recent has been published. The grove's other named giant, the Adam Tree, held the title of largest in the grove until Genesis was measured in 1985. Neither tree has a published age.
mountain-home-state-forest.question_meta: Genesis, a giant sequoia once ranked seventh-largest on Earth, stands burned but alive in Mountain Home Grove after the 2020 Castle Fire.
mountain-home-state-forest.question_context: Mountain Home Grove lies in Mountain Home Demonstration State Forest, run by CAL FIRE, in the mountains of Tulare County above the town of Springville. The surrounding land is a patchwork of the state forest, Balch Park and Giant Sequoia National Monument. There is no bus and no shortcut: the way in is by car on mountain roads, and the condition of those roads and of the trails to the two named trees changes with the season and with the aftermath of the 2020 Castle Fire, so check with CAL FIRE or Tulare County before setting out. Entry is free. The Adam Tree stands to the north of Genesis, a few kilometres apart within the grove, and between them they tell the fire's story from both sides: one tree that lost its crown, one that was barely touched. Adam was named around 1884 by Jesse Hoskins and was the grove's largest until Genesis was measured in 1985. Both pins are approximate, and neither tree has a published age. The latest visitor reports date from 2021, so anyone who walks the grove now sees more than we can tell you.

faq.q: What is the largest tree in Mountain Home Grove?
faq.a: Genesis, a giant sequoia measured in 2013 at 86.2 metres tall and 24.04 metres round. Those are pre-fire figures: the 2020 Castle Fire took its top, so it is shorter today by an amount nobody has published.

faq.q: Did the Castle Fire kill the sequoias at Mountain Home?
faq.a: Not the two named here. Visitors in 2021 found Genesis badly damaged but alive and the Adam Tree nearly untouched. We have found no report on either since 2023.

faq.q: Is it free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. The grove is in a state forest with no entry fee. It is reached by car from Springville; check road and trail status with CAL FIRE before you go.

stanislaus-national-forest.intro: The largest known juniper in the United States stands in Sardine Meadow, at the end of a rough Forest Service road in the Stanislaus National Forest. The Bennett Juniper is about 3.9 metres across and 24 metres tall, and cores taken in the 1930s and again in 1989 both put it near 3,000 years, though the hollow trunk keeps the full count out of reach. It survived the 2018 Donnell Fire, and since 2022 its three acres belong to the Mother Lode Land Trust.
stanislaus-national-forest.meta_description: The Bennett Juniper in Stanislaus National Forest is the largest known juniper in the US, cored at close to 3,000 years old.
stanislaus-national-forest.question_answer: The oldest tree in Stanislaus National Forest that we map is the Bennett Juniper, a grand juniper in Sardine Meadow cored at about 3,000 years. A core taken in the 1930s gave about 3,000; a second in 1989 gave almost 3,000. The trunk is partly hollow, so neither reached the centre, and the man it is named after believed it was over 6,000, by extrapolation rather than measurement. By the American Forests points formula it is the largest known juniper in the United States, about 3.9 metres across and 24 metres tall.
stanislaus-national-forest.question_meta: The Bennett Juniper, cored at close to 3,000 years, is the largest known juniper in the US, in Sardine Meadow, Stanislaus National Forest.
stanislaus-national-forest.question_context: The Bennett Juniper stands in Sardine Meadow, on a three-acre preserve that is a private inholding inside Stanislaus National Forest. The Mother Lode Land Trust has owned it since November 2022, and entry is free. Getting there is the hard part. From the Pinecrest side you follow Forest Service road 5N01 and then the unpaved 5N83Y and 5N83YB to a pull-around, where a short signed path leads to the tree. A high-clearance vehicle is needed, and snow closes the road in winter; one listing gives the season as mid-April to mid-December, though we have only seen that secondhand. There is no public transport. When the Forest Service ran a field trip to the tree in October 2025, it set out from the Summit Ranger Station at Pinecrest. The tree came through the 2018 Donnell Fire. What waits at the end is the largest known juniper in the United States, about 3.9 metres across and 24 metres tall, cored at close to 3,000 years. It was long counted a western juniper and is now placed in the grand juniper; one book calls it a mountain juniper.

faq.q: How old is the Bennett Juniper?
faq.a: Close to 3,000 years by two cores, one from the 1930s and one from 1989. The trunk is partly hollow, so a full count is impossible, and older claims of 6,000 years rest on extrapolation.

faq.q: Can you drive to the Bennett Juniper?
faq.a: Almost. Unpaved Forest Service roads lead to a pull-around with a short walking path to the tree. You need high clearance, and snow closes the road in winter.

faq.q: Who owns the Bennett Juniper?
faq.a: The Mother Lode Land Trust, since November 2022. The three-acre preserve sits inside Stanislaus National Forest and is free to visit.

logan-canyon.intro: The Jardine Juniper is often said to be 3,000 years old. Cores taken in the 1950s said about 1,500. It is a Rocky Mountain juniper only about 12 metres tall with a trunk 7.2 metres round, found in 1923 on a ridge above Logan Canyon, and the walk to it is a day: about 11 miles there and back from Wood Camp on US-89.
logan-canyon.meta_description: The Jardine Juniper above Logan Canyon, Utah, is about 1,500 years old by its cores: an 11-mile round-trip hike from Wood Camp on US-89.
logan-canyon.question_answer: The oldest tree in Logan Canyon is the Jardine Juniper, a Rocky Mountain juniper about 1,500 years old by cores taken in the 1950s. It is often credited with 3,000 years, but the cores do not support that. The tree is about 12 metres tall with a trunk 7.2 metres round, and it was found in 1923 by Maurice Blood Linford. Visit Utah reports a small bunch of greenery still alive in its upper branches; that report is undated, and we have found no dated sighting since 2020.
logan-canyon.question_meta: Logan Canyon's oldest tree is the Jardine Juniper, about 1,500 years old by its cores, still showing green in an undated report.
logan-canyon.question_context: The Jardine Juniper Trail starts at the Wood Camp Campground trailhead on US-89, a drive up Logan Canyon from the city of Logan, Utah. There is no public transport up the canyon, and parking at the trailhead is paid. Visit Utah gives the hike as about 11 miles there and back with roughly 2,145 feet of elevation gain. The tree itself is only about 2.5 kilometres from the trailhead in a straight line, so treat the mileage as Visit Utah's figure for the trail as walked; the route was realigned by the Forest Service in recent years. The trail is open all year, but in spring 2026 hikers reported snow and mud lingering on the shady side. Do not expect a tall tree at the top. The Jardine Juniper is about 12 metres high; what stops people is the trunk, 7.2 metres round, on a tree about 1,500 years old by cores taken in the 1950s. Maurice Blood Linford found it in 1923. The latest word on its health is an undated report of a small bunch of green in the upper branches, so a dated report from anyone who makes the climb is worth more than usual.

faq.q: Is the Jardine Juniper still alive?
faq.a: As far as we know. Visit Utah reports a small bunch of green in the upper branches, but the report is undated, and we have found no dated sighting since 2020.

faq.q: How long is the hike to the Jardine Juniper?
faq.a: About 11 miles round trip with roughly 2,145 feet of gain, starting from the Wood Camp Campground trailhead on US-89 in Logan Canyon. Parking there is paid.

faq.q: Is the Jardine Juniper 3,000 years old?
faq.a: Probably not. That figure is often repeated, but cores taken in the 1950s indicated about 1,500 years.

leggett.intro: Leggett is where US-101 meets a coast redwood with a road through it. The Chandelier Tree is 84 metres tall by laser, rather less than the 315 feet its sign claims, and in the late 1930s the Underwood family cut a tunnel through its base, 6 feet wide and 6 feet 9 inches high, wide enough for a car. It has been a paid roadside stop ever since, in a private park open every day of the year but Christmas and Thanksgiving.
leggett.meta_description: The Chandelier Tree at Leggett is an 84-metre coast redwood with a car tunnel cut through its base in the late 1930s.
leggett.question_answer: The tree Leggett is known for is the Chandelier Tree, a coast redwood 84 metres tall by laser rangefinder, with a tunnel cut through its base in the late 1930s that cars can drive through. The sign at the park claims 315 feet in height and 21 feet in width; modern measurements give 276 feet and 16 feet across at chest height. An age of 2,400 years is often quoted but we could not trace it to a source. The name comes from limbs 4 to 7 feet thick that branch out from about 100 feet up.
leggett.question_meta: Leggett's Chandelier Tree is an 84-metre coast redwood with a 1930s car tunnel through its base, in a private park on US-101.
leggett.question_context: The Chandelier Tree stands in Drive-Thru Tree Park, a privately owned park at 67402 Drive Thru Tree Road, Leggett, just off US-101 in Mendocino County where the highway meets CA-271. There is no public transport; nearly everyone arrives by car, and the car is the point. The tunnel through the base is 6 feet wide and 6 feet 9 inches high, cut in the late 1930s by the Underwood family, who had bought the grove in 1921. Cutting it damaged the tree, and it has also made the place a roadside stop for close to ninety years. Larger vehicles may not fit, and there is a separate fee for walking through on foot. The park opens daily except Christmas and Thanksgiving. One listing gives $15 a car, with hours from 8:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. in summer and to 5 p.m. off-season; these come from secondhand listings rather than the owners, so call 707-925-6363 before you rely on them. Look up once you are through: the limbs that give the tree its name, 4 to 7 feet thick, branch out from about 100 feet. A road blog found the tree standing and the park busy in July 2026.

faq.q: Can you still drive through the Chandelier Tree?
faq.a: Yes. It is the park's attraction and the tree was standing and open to visitors in July 2026. The tunnel is 6 feet wide and 6 feet 9 inches high, so larger vehicles may not fit.

faq.q: How tall is the Chandelier Tree?
faq.a: About 84 metres, 276 feet, by laser rangefinder. The park's sign says 315 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost?
faq.a: Entry is paid. One listing gives $15 per car, with a separate fee for pedestrians; call the park on 707-925-6363 to confirm. It is closed on Christmas and Thanksgiving.

mobile.intro: Mobile's best-known tree comes with a hanging. Charles Boyington, a printer executed on 20 February 1835 for the murder of Nathaniel Frost, swore an oak would grow from his heart to prove his innocence, and the live oak by the Church Street Graveyard is the one the city has pointed to ever since. The cemetery wall was moved back after 1900, so the Boyington Oak now stands outside it on Bayou Street, free to see, with its own festival every May.
mobile.meta_description: The Boyington Oak in Mobile, Alabama, is the live oak said to have grown from a hanged man's grave in 1835, outside the Church Street Graveyard.
mobile.question_answer: The tree Mobile is known for is the Boyington Oak, a southern live oak on Bayou Street just outside the wall of the Church Street Graveyard. By the city's legend it grew from the grave of Charles Boyington, hanged in 1835 for a murder he swore he did not commit, who said an oak would rise from his heart as proof. The hanging is on record; the link to the tree is folklore. Nobody has dated the oak, so its age is open. It was still standing in May 2025, when Mobile held its sixth annual Boyington Oak Festival.
mobile.question_meta: Mobile's Boyington Oak stands outside the Church Street Graveyard, the live oak of a legend about a printer hanged in 1835.
mobile.question_context: The Boyington Oak stands in downtown Mobile, at the Church Street Graveyard, whose address is 106 South Scott Street. The tree is not inside the cemetery. When the wall was moved back after 1900, the oak ended up on the outside, at the edge of Bayou Street, so you can see it from the public street at any hour without passing a gate. The graveyard itself offers free city walking tours that start from its Scott Street gate, and the oak is a short walk from there along the wall. Downtown is walkable; we have not checked the nearest bus stop. The legend is the reason to come. Charles Boyington, a printer, was hanged on 20 February 1835 for the murder of Nathaniel Frost and buried in the potter's field corner of this graveyard, swearing that an oak would grow from his heart to prove him innocent. The hanging is on record; the link between his grave and this tree is folklore, and nobody has dated the oak. Ghost stories attach to it freely. Each May Mobile holds a Boyington Oak Festival, and the sixth, in 2025, included a trolley ride out to the tree.

faq.q: Is the Boyington Oak inside the cemetery?
faq.a: No. It stands just outside the wall of the Church Street Graveyard, on the edge of Bayou Street, because the wall was moved back after 1900.

faq.q: Did the oak really grow from Charles Boyington's grave?
faq.a: That is the legend. Boyington was hanged in 1835 and buried in the graveyard's potter's field corner, but no ring count or record ties the tree to his grave.

faq.q: Is it free to see?
faq.a: Yes. It is visible from the public street, and the graveyard runs free walking tours from its Scott Street gate.

long-beach-mississippi.intro: The Friendship Oak has lost all its leaves to two hurricanes, Camille and Katrina, and is still here at more than 500 years old by the University of Southern Mississippi's count. It stands on the university's Gulf Park campus in Long Beach, a southern live oak 59 feet tall with a crown 155 feet across. Its trunk was 14 feet round when it joined the Live Oak Society around 1940 and 19.8 feet when the state measured it in 2011.
long-beach-mississippi.meta_description: The Friendship Oak in Long Beach, Mississippi, is a live oak over 500 years old that survived Camille and Katrina, on USM's Gulf Park campus.
long-beach-mississippi.question_answer: The oldest tree in Long Beach, Mississippi, is the Friendship Oak, a southern live oak the University of Southern Mississippi puts at more than 500 years old. It stands on the university's Gulf Park campus, 59 feet tall with a trunk 19.8 feet round and a crown 155 feet across, by a 2011 state measurement. Hurricanes Camille and Katrina both stripped it of leaves; a limb broke in 2017 and the tree has been braced since. It is member 110 of the Live Oak Society.
long-beach-mississippi.question_meta: The Friendship Oak, over 500 years old, stands on USM's Gulf Park campus in Long Beach, Mississippi, after two hurricanes stripped it bare.
long-beach-mississippi.question_context: The Friendship Oak stands at Friendship Oak Circle on the Avenue of the Oaks, on the University of Southern Mississippi's Gulf Park campus in Long Beach. The campus grounds are open rather than gated, and no visiting hours are published, so the tree is there whenever you are. In March 2025 the university finished a beautification project around it: new sidewalks, lighting, benches and an off-street viewing area, meant in its words as a welcoming space for students, faculty and visitors. The ribbon-cutting crowd that month toured the tree. There is no fee. Most people come by car along the Mississippi Gulf Coast; we have not checked a bus route. What you will see is a southern live oak 59 feet tall with a crown 155 feet across, which is wider than the tree is tall by a long way. Look for the bracing: a limb broke off in August 2017 and the tree has been supported since. It joined the Live Oak Society around 1940 as member 110, when its trunk measured 14 feet round; by 2011 that was 19.8 feet. Hurricanes Camille and Katrina both stripped it of its leaves, and both times it grew them back.

faq.q: How old is the Friendship Oak?
faq.a: More than 500 years, according to the University of Southern Mississippi, on whose campus it stands.

faq.q: Can visitors see the Friendship Oak?
faq.a: Yes. It is on open campus grounds at Friendship Oak Circle, with a viewing area, benches and lighting added in 2025. There is no fee.

faq.q: Did Hurricane Katrina damage the Friendship Oak?
faq.a: Katrina stripped its leaves, as Camille had before it, and the tree recovered both times. A limb broke in 2017 and has been braced.

thomasville.intro: Thomasville bought a corner lot in 1966 to give one live oak a park of its own. The Big Oak has stood at Crawford and Monroe streets since around 1680, by the local history centre's estimate, and its crown now spreads 169 feet. Trucks have taken limbs off it three times. The city answers with cables, columns, lightning protection, a yearly inspection and a phone number that triggers a camera across the street, so visitors can photograph themselves beneath it.
thomasville.meta_description: Thomasville's Big Oak is a live oak of over 300 years with a 169-foot crown, in its own downtown park since 1966.
thomasville.question_answer: The oldest tree in Thomasville is the Big Oak, a southern live oak dated to around 1680 by the Thomasville History Center's curator, who says the date is not exact; call it over 300 years. It stands in Elizabeth Ireland Poe Park at Crawford and Monroe streets downtown, with a crown spreading 169 feet, a height of about 72 feet and a trunk close to 28 feet round. It joined the Live Oak Society in 1936 as its 49th member.
thomasville.question_meta: Thomasville's oldest tree is the Big Oak, a live oak dated to around 1680, with a 169-foot crown at Crawford and Monroe streets.
thomasville.question_context: The Big Oak has a small park to itself, Elizabeth Ireland Poe Park, at the corner of Crawford and Monroe streets in downtown Thomasville, Georgia. The city bought the lot in 1966 to make the park. It is free and open, with no gate, and there is no public transport to speak of; street parking is the usual approach, though we have not confirmed the nearest spaces. Traffic has been the tree's real enemy: trucks clipped its limbs in 1973, in 1975 and again in 2005. Today city Public Works and arborists inspect it every year and keep it on cables and columns, with a lightning protection system. Look for the posted phone number. Dial it and a remote camera across the street takes a keepsake photograph of you under the tree. The crown spreads 169 feet and the tree stands about 72 feet tall. The marker gives the girth as 27.5 feet, other sources nearer 28; heights also vary by source. It joined the Live Oak Society in 1936 as its 49th member, when the trunk measured 21 feet 6 inches round. The local history centre dates it to around 1680, while saying the date is not exact.

faq.q: How old is the Big Oak in Thomasville?
faq.a: Over 300 years. The Thomasville History Center's curator dates it to around 1680, while saying the date is not exact.

faq.q: How big is the Big Oak?
faq.a: Its crown spreads 169 feet and it stands about 72 feet tall, with a trunk close to 28 feet round. Figures vary a little between sources and the marker.

faq.q: Was the Big Oak a lynching tree?
faq.a: No. Local historian Jack Hadley has said it was not.

goose-island-state-park.intro: The Big Tree at Goose Island is a live oak over 1,000 years old by the Texas Forest Service, and nearer 2,000 by other recent estimates. Its trunk is more than 35 feet round and its crown spreads about 90 feet. It was the Texas state champion live oak from 1969 to 2003, and Texas Parks and Wildlife counts it among the largest live oaks in the country. Hurricane Harvey passed over in 2017 and left it relatively unscathed.
goose-island-state-park.meta_description: The Big Tree in Goose Island State Park, Texas, is a live oak over 1,000 years old, state champion from 1969 to 2003.
goose-island-state-park.question_answer: The oldest tree in Goose Island State Park is the Big Tree, a southern live oak the Texas Forest Service estimates at over 1,000 years old; other recent estimates put it nearer 2,000. Its trunk is more than 35 feet round, it stands over 45 feet tall and its crown spreads about 90 feet. It held the Texas state champion title for live oaks from 1969 to 2003 and was a charter member of the Live Oak Society. Locals also call it the Bishop Oak or the Lamar Oak.
goose-island-state-park.question_meta: Goose Island State Park's Big Tree is a live oak over 1,000 years old, possibly nearer 2,000, and a former Texas champion.
goose-island-state-park.question_context: The Big Tree stands in Goose Island State Park, at 3918 Park Road 13, north of Rockport. It is in the park's Lamar section, which is why some locals call it the Lamar Oak; others know it as the Bishop Oak. You reach it by car, since no public transport runs out here, and the tree is right beside the park road with parking next to it, so the walk is a matter of steps rather than miles. A fence rings the base to keep feet off the roots, but the crown spreads about 90 feet, well past the fence, and visitors can stand underneath it. An older newspaper account describes rangers opening a gate for visitors; that arrangement may have changed, so expect the fence. The park opens daily from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m., and entry is $5 for adults and free for children under 13. The tree came through Hurricane Harvey in August 2017 relatively unscathed, and Texas Parks and Wildlife still lists it among the largest live oaks in the United States. Its age stays a range rather than a number: over 1,000 years by the Texas Forest Service, nearer 2,000 by other estimates.

faq.q: How old is the Big Tree at Goose Island?
faq.a: Over 1,000 years by the Texas Forest Service's estimate; other recent estimates say closer to 2,000. The sources do not agree on a single figure.

faq.q: Can you walk under the Big Tree?
faq.a: Yes. The base is fenced to protect the roots, but you can stand beneath the crown.

faq.q: Does it cost money to see the Big Tree?
faq.a: It is inside Goose Island State Park, where entry is $5 for adults and free for children under 13. The park is open daily from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.

oroville.intro: Oroville's Mother Orange Tree has been dug up and moved twice, the second time in 1964 to make way for the Oroville Dam. It is a Mediterranean sweet orange from Mazatlan, bought in Sacramento in 1856 and planted in 1856 by its plaque, or 1854 by one other account. The 1998 frost hollowed its trunk and stopped the fruit for a time; the fruit came back, and in 2003 UC Riverside cloned it. It is California Historical Landmark number 1043.
oroville.meta_description: The Mother Orange Tree in Oroville is a sweet orange from the 1850s, moved twice and cloned in 2003, now at the State Parks office.
oroville.question_answer: The oldest tree in Oroville is the Mother Orange Tree, a sweet orange planted in the 1850s, in 1854 by one account and 1856 by its plaque. It was bought in Sacramento in 1856 by Judge Joseph Lewis, moved in 1862 and again in 1964 for the Oroville Dam, and now stands outside the California State Parks office at 400 Glen Drive. The most recent account of its health is a visitor's from September 2021, who found it healthy and green.
oroville.question_meta: Oroville's oldest tree is the Mother Orange Tree, a sweet orange from the 1850s at the State Parks office on Glen Drive.
oroville.question_context: The Mother Orange Tree stands at the entrance of the California State Parks district office at 400 Glen Drive in Oroville, Butte County, and a sign on Glen Drive points the way. It is free to see and outdoors, so the office's opening hours do not decide when you can visit. A fence keeps visitors a short distance back from the trunk. The oranges on the branches are not for picking; a visitor in 2021 found that fallen fruit on the ground was treated as fair game. We have not checked public transport, so plan on a car. The tree has not always stood here. It was bought in Sacramento in 1856, moved in 1862, and moved again in 1964 to make way for the Oroville Dam. After the 1998 frost, decay fungus hollowed the trunk and the fruit stopped for a time before coming back; in 2003 UC Riverside cloned it. It is California Historical Landmark number 1043. Its planting year is 1856 on the plaque and 1854 in one other account. Our latest report of its health is that visitor's from September 2021, who found it healthy and green, so a fresh one is welcome.

faq.q: How old is the Mother Orange Tree?
faq.a: About 170 years. It was planted in 1854 according to one account and in 1856 according to the plaque.

faq.q: Where is the Mother Orange Tree?
faq.a: Outside the California State Parks office at 400 Glen Drive in Oroville. It was moved there in 1964, when the Oroville Dam was built.

faq.q: Can I pick an orange from the Mother Orange Tree?
faq.a: No. The tree is fenced and its fruit is not for picking.

riverside.intro: Riverside has made city landmarks of four of its trees, and each one has a name attached. Eliza Tibbets planted the Parent Washington Navel Orange Tree in 1873; it now lives in a 22-foot insect-screen tent. The Chicago White Sox planted a redwood in Low Park in 1914, 400 metres away. Theodore Roosevelt planted a palm on Victoria Avenue in 1903. And a sycamore on a median island near Fairmount Park is a landmark nobody has explained. Together they make a short drive across the city, with the first two an easy walk apart.
riverside.meta_description: Four Riverside landmark trees: the 1873 Parent Navel Orange, the White Sox redwood of 1914, Roosevelt's 1903 palm and a native sycamore.
riverside.question_answer: The oldest tree in Riverside that we map is the Parent Washington Navel Orange Tree, about 150 years old, planted by Eliza Tibbets in 1873 at what is now the corner of Magnolia and Arlington avenues. It is California Historical Landmark number 20, maintained by UC Riverside and the city, and still bearing fruit at the December 2025 harvest. Since 2019 it has stood inside a 22-foot insect-screen tent to keep out citrus greening disease, so you see it through the screen.
riverside.question_meta: Riverside's oldest mapped tree is the Parent Navel Orange Tree, planted by Eliza Tibbets in 1873, now in a screen tent on Magnolia Avenue.
riverside.question_context: The four landmark trees spread across Riverside, and all four are free and on public ground. Start at the corner of Magnolia and Arlington avenues, where the Parent Navel Orange Tree stands in a small city landmark plot looked after by UC Riverside and the city's Parks Department. Since June 2019 it has lived inside a 22-foot insect-screen tent against citrus greening disease, so you see it through the screen; older photographs show it without. About 400 metres away, Low Park sits at the head of Magnolia and Palm avenues, and the Chicago White Sox Redwood Tree stands there beside the tablet Charles Comiskey added in 1927. The Roosevelt Palm is about three kilometres off on Victoria Avenue near Myrtle Street, a street listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and it shares a small plot with five other palms; look for the 1965 tablet at its foot. The Native Sycamore stands on a median island where La Paz Lane meets Bubbling Well Road, by Fairmount Park, about six kilometres north of the orange. See it from the pavement, since crossing to the island means stepping into traffic. We have not checked bus routes between them.

faq.q: Where is the original navel orange tree?
faq.a: At the corner of Magnolia and Arlington avenues in Riverside, inside a 22-foot insect-screen tent since 2019. Eliza Tibbets planted it in 1873.

faq.q: Which palm did Theodore Roosevelt plant in Riverside?
faq.a: The Roosevelt Palm on Victoria Avenue near Myrtle Street, planted on 7 May 1903. It stands with five other palms; it is the one over the 1965 tablet.

faq.q: Why is there a White Sox tree in Riverside?
faq.a: Chicago White Sox players planted a redwood in Low Park in 1914, after an exhibition game in the city. Owner Charles Comiskey added a tablet in 1927.

faq.q: Are Riverside's landmark trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. All four are on public ground: a landmark plot, a city park, a street frontage and a median island.
